newsitem.title: CHILE: Chile may allow its banks to lend overseas.
newsitem.headline: Chile may allow its banks to lend overseas.

text.p: The Central Bank will start changing Chilean financial codes to allow private banks to start overseas lending after Congress passes a bill regulating banking activity -- or shortly before, a key Central Bank official said.
Two obstacles would have to be overcome before the Central Bank could start looking at regulatory changes to allow banks to lend to foreign clients, he said.

First, private banks would have to finish rescheduling payments on their private debts to the Central Bank, and second, Congress would have to pass the Banking Law redefining the sector's regulatory framework, said the official.

"As soon as that happens, and it's a few months away, we'll start working immediately on taking measures ... to allow Chilean banks to lend in foreign markets," said the official, who declined to be named. The changes could also start shortly before congressional approval, he said.
Chilean private banks have long sought legal changes to allow them to branch out into foreign lending.
The new Banking Law has been passed by the Chamber of Deputies but not the Senate.
The official said that after barriers to foreign lending were lifted, the banks would still need time to develop expertise in the business.
"That's going to take a couple of years. Don't expect Chilean banks to start lending to all of Latin America overnight," he said.
Chile's currently-conservative banking laws are aimed at preventing another financial crash like that which nearly wiped out the industry in the early 1980s.
During that episode, the Central Bank had to intervene with billions of dollars in loans.

Most private banks have rescheduled and refinanced their debts to the Central Bank, with the soon-to-be-merged Banco O'Higgins and Banco de Santiago the only institutions whose repayment plans still await final approval.

The Central Bank official said once banks started foreign lending, money obtained by them overseas and then relent outside Chile would probably not be affected by the "encaje," the 30 percent reserve requirement for some investments coming into Chile.
"The encaje is for financial, short-term investments in Chile, not those that enter only as a step to be invested abroad," said the official. But he said the issue was still under study.
